itemsBuilt.title: Read-only DB loader
itemsBuilt.description: loadCountyParcelRecords(sql, countyFips) — two indexed, county-filtered SELECTs (parcel_record; parcel_record_cell JOIN parcel_record) via a minimal duck-typed SQL-client interface (ParcelRecordSqlClient, matching the callable shape of a `postgres()` instance already used elsewhere in this package). Maps rows into ParcelRecordRow[] and calls the existing assertFullRecordCells on every record, so a parcel_record row with an incomplete rail-cell set throws loudly ("missing rail column: X") instead of silently defaulting -- row-absence is never treated as the stored 'unaccounted' sentinel. Exported through index.ts. Never issues a write; never closes the caller's connection (caller owns session lifecycle).

loaderPerformanceFinding.headline: 101.5s to load the SMALLEST of the six counties (24,988 parcels / 1.62M cell rows) contradicts CP1 stepF's 'low risk -- pure read' framing for the loader specifically, though not for the gate logic it was really about.
loaderPerformanceFinding.mechanism: CP1's sixCountyPlan cost estimate ('cheap and safe... under 10 seconds') was measured against a fundamentally different, cheaper query shape: server-side aggregate GROUP BY queries returning a handful of (kind, count) rows. A real loader must materialize every individual cell row client-side to reconstruct ParcelRecordRow[] -- roughly 1.6M JSONB rows for the smallest county alone. That is not the same cost class, and CP1's own numbers should not have been read as validating loader performance, only aggregate-query performance. Naming this rather than letting CP1's 'cheap and safe' framing stand unqualified into CP2's own work.
loaderPerformanceFinding.rejectedAlternativeMechanism: Concurrent Cloud Run writer-job contention (per CP1's movingTargetWarning) is a plausible second explanation for slow reads on this table, but this session did not run EXPLAIN or inspect lock waits, so it is not confirmed and is not asserted as the cause here -- named as unconfirmed, not ruled in.
loaderPerformanceFinding.scalingImplication: At this measured ~16,000 rows/sec, the largest county (48453, 380,917 parcels / ~24.76M cells) would be on the order of 25+ minutes for a single-shot full load -- a materially different feasibility class than the smallest county, and untested this checkpoint. Not fixed or optimized here (out of CP2 scope: prove correctness on one small county, which is done); carried forward as a leave_behind for whoever builds the real hauska-factory publish-time caller.

warnCrossCheck.design: Additive-only, opt-in. PublishGateOptions gained priorLiveRailKeys?: readonly ParcelRecordRailKey[] (rails known live as of a prior evaluation, supplied by the caller -- this module holds no history of its own). PublishGateVerdict gained a REQUIRED warnings: PublishGateWarning[] field (mirrors the existing required-field pattern already enforced by the file's own ts-expect-error compile-check test for excludedDeclaredAhead). For every rail in excludedDeclaredAhead that IS in the caller-supplied priorLiveRailKeys, evaluatePublishGate now emits { kind: 'full-rail-poison', railKey, detail }. Omitting the option (the default, and every existing call site) produces zero warnings -- behavior for every pre-existing caller is unchanged.
warnCrossCheck.decision: accept-and-warn, not a new acquisition-status registry -- matches the lane planner's CP2 scoping decision exactly; not re-litigated.
newTests: "full-rail poison stays silent without prior-state info (opt-in only, no regression)" -- fully poisons a rail with no priorLiveRailKeys given; asserts excludedDeclaredAhead contains it AND warnings.length === 0. Proves the additive change cannot surprise an existing caller.

"warns when a rail goes from live to fully poisoned, given prior liveness (WARN cross-check)" -- two records both carrying an earned 'apn' cell (rail live); captures priorLiveRailKeys from that verdict; poisons EVERY earned 'apn' cell across both records; re-evaluates WITH priorLiveRailKeys; asserts the rail is now excludedDeclaredAhead AND carries a warnings entry with kind='full-rail-poison' and the right railKey; also asserts a genuinely-never-attempted declared-ahead rail ('owner') does NOT warn, proving the check is specific to rails that went from live to poisoned, not every declared-ahead rail.
warnCrossCheck.existingTestUnchanged: "poisoning the last earned cell of a rail demotes it (known limit)" was NOT modified -- runs and passes exactly as before, now implicitly also demonstrating the default warnings:[] via the interface's required field, without needing to be touched.

LESSON: A worktree reporting a clean test pass earlier in the SAME session is not proof node_modules is still installed later in that session -- always check `ls node_modules` (or run the exact pinned-version check) before trusting a vitest/tsc invocation's version, especially after any gap between checkpoints. npx will silently auto-install an unpinned major version rather than failing loud when a package is missing but the command name resolves.

An aggregate GROUP BY query's timing tells you almost nothing about a row-materializing SELECT's timing over the same table -- CP1's 'cheap and safe, under 10 seconds' cost estimate for six sequential county reads was true for the query CP1 actually ran (aggregates) and not transferable to a real loader that must pull every individual cell row client-side. Always re-measure the SPECIFIC query shape a new consumer will actually issue.

A dispatch's 'add as a rail OR name a concrete structural reason not to' escape hatch is worth taking seriously rather than defaulting to the safer-looking 'just add it' path -- reading the actual already-committed schema doc for the CAD-SERVE-RECONCILE fields (a p63-verdict-serve CP1 artifact already in doc_repo, no new repo needed) surfaced a real duplication risk that a shallower read would have missed.

pnpm's --filter <pkg>... scoped install pulls only that package's OWN dependency graph, not its sibling packages' dev/test dependency closures in the same monorepo -- a scoped install can leave OTHER packages' test files still unresolvable even after it succeeds cleanly. Don't read a scoped install's success as 'the whole monorepo's tests are now runnable.'
